findings.issue_text: [BUG] Deleting `p := prometheus.NewRegistry()` while the next line still calls `NewDualWriter(Mode1, ls, us, p)` leaves `p` undefined, so the package does not compile. go build/vet of pkg/apiserver/rest fails with "undefined: p"; every test in the package (modes 0-3) and CI is blocked by this diff unless `p` is declared elsewhere in the same test package, which this diff does not add.

[BUG] TestMode3_Create and the Delete/DeleteCollection tests use bare `p` in `NewDualWriter(Mode3, ls, us, p)` with no declaration of `p` in those functions (only TestMode3_Get declares its own local `p`), so the test file only compiles if a package-level `p` exists that this diff never adds. `go test ./pkg/apiserver/rest` fails to compile with "undefined: p" for TestMode3_Create, TestMode3_List, TestMode3_Delete, TestMode3_DeleteCollection and TestMode3_Update; the whole suite is red.

[BUG] The "error when creating object in the unified store fails" test case only registers a mock for legacy `Create` and never registers `m.On("Create", ...)` for the storage mock, but DualWriterMode3.Create calls d.Storage.Create first, so testify's mock.Mock panics with "mock: I don't know what to return". The new Mode3 Create error-path test crashes the test binary instead of asserting the error, so the wantErr branch is never validated and the package test run aborts.

[BUG] TestMode3_Delete and TestMode3_DeleteCollection set up only storage mocks, but Mode3.Delete/DeleteCollection now spawn a goroutine calling d.Legacy.Delete / d.Legacy.DeleteCollection on the same unmocked mock.Mock, which panics. The legacy-delete goroutine panics inside `go func(){...}` and crashes the whole test process (unrecovered goroutine panic), failing TestMode3_Delete/TestMode3_DeleteCollection non-deterministically after the storage assertions pass.

[BUG] DualWriterMode3.Update's storage-error path calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` instead of recordStorageDuration, so a failed unified-store update is recorded as a legacy-storage failure metric. Anyone using the dual-writer duration/error metrics to debug unified storage outages sees legacy-storage error counts increment for storage failures, pointing operators at the wrong backend during incidents.

[BUG] DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine records the legacy deletion result with `d.recordStorageDuration(...)` instead of recordLegacyDuration. All legacy DeleteCollection latency and error samples in Mode3 are emitted under storage duration/label metrics, corrupting the unified-storage latency histogram and hiding legacy failures from dashboards.

[BUG] Delete's success path calls `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passing the object `name` where every other call site passes `options.Kind` as the kind label. Mode3 delete metrics get per-object-name "kind" labels, exploding the label cardinality of the metric and making delete metrics unqueryable by kind.

[BUG] Delete does `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` instead of `klog.NewContext(ctx, log)`, discarding the enriched logger (name/kind/method values) it just built. Delete-path structured log lines and the goroutine's derived ctx lose the name/kind/method fields, degrading incident debugging for Mode3 deletes specifically while every other method logs with enrichment.

[ADVISORY] The legacy write goroutines in Create/Update share the caller's `obj` (and objInfo/options in Update) with the synchronous storage write and the returned object without any synchronization, and return to the caller immediately. This is a data race under `go test -race` and in production: the API caller or Storage.Create mutates the object after Create returns while the goroutine still reads it; the race detector in CI will flake, and real concurrent mutation can send a torn or already-modified object to legacy storage, breaking dual-write consistency guarantees.

[ADVISORY] Mode3.Create previously guaranteed (best-effort synchronous) legacy write before returning; making legacy writes fire-and-forget goroutines with only a log on error means any legacy failure is now unobservable and unretryable by the caller. Operators running mode 3 during a legacy-storage outage get silent divergence between unified and legacy stores with no reconciliation hook, and tests (and downstream consumers like the playlist integration tests) that read legacy storage immediately after a create can observe the object missing — the new file/etcd mode-3 integration tests in this diff will flake on this timing window.

[ADVISORY] The three copy-pasted goroutine blocks (Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection) each hand-maintain their own timeout construction, metric call, and context wrapping, and they have already drifted (DeleteCollection records storage metrics, Delete passes `name` as kind), showing the parallel structure is unsafe to modify. The next change to legacy-write behavior (e.g., adding retry or changing the metric) must be replicated in four places; this diff itself shipped three metric/log inconsistencies in exactly this way, which is direct evidence the next maintainer gets bitten too.

[BUG] The fire-and-forget goroutine performing the legacy Create (and the same pattern in Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection) derives its 10s-timeout context from the incoming request context, which the apiserver cancels as soon as the HTTP request returns. Every legacy write on a fast or slow request path races the request-context cancellation; when the request completes first the legacy Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection is aborted mid-flight, so Mode 3 silently stops dual-writing and the two stores diverge with no error surfaced to the caller or the logs — the exact consistency guarantee Mode 3 exists to provide is dropped.

[BUG] Create's storage-failure path calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) instead of recordStorageDuration, and Update's storage-failure path (line ~120) does the same, while Delete's success path passes `name` where every other call passes `options.Kind` as the kind label. Prometheus metrics for Mode 3 are recorded against the wrong status label (legacy instead of storage) and wrong kind label (object name instead of resource kind), so the dual-writer dashboards/alerts added alongside this change report fabricated legacy-write failures for every failed storage create/update and unqueryable kind labels for deletes.

[BUG] DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine calls d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...) for a LegacyStorage call, recording legacy-write latency under the storage metric. Legacy delete-collection latency is attributed to the unified-storage metric, corrupting the storage-health signal operators use to decide when it is safe to migrate off dual-write mode.

[ADVISORY] Update now passes the raw objInfo to the async Legacy.Update instead of the previous updateWrapper that pinned the object actually written to Storage, so legacy recomputes the updated object from its own (possibly stale) old object. During the dual-write migration window, a concurrent update between the Storage write and the legacy goroutine's read causes legacy to persist a different object than Storage computed from the same request — the updateWrapper existed precisely to prevent this divergence and its removal is undocumented and untested.

[ADVISORY] No test in this diff verifies the defining Mode 3 behavior that writes reach LegacyStorage: the goroutines are asynchronous and testify mocks are never asserted (no m.AssertExpectations / AssertNotCalled / wait), so a regression that drops the legacy write entirely still passes all TestMode3_* cases. A future refactor that deletes the legacy goroutines — silently turning Mode 3 into Storage-only writes — is green in CI and in the playlist integration tests that only read from unified storage; the mode's core acceptance criterion (dual write) is unverified.

[ADVISORY] Delete's legacy goroutine is skipped entirely when the Storage delete errors, dropping the previous behavior (commented-out code) of still attempting the legacy delete on non-NotFound storage errors, and the sync log.WithValues("name", name) was replaced with klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) that omits name/kind from the actual logger used. Operators grepping delete failures for the affected object name get log lines without it, and a partial-failure state (deleted in one store) now has no attempt to converge the other store.

[BUG] Create's legacy write runs in a fire-and-forget goroutine whose context is derived from the request ctx, so when the API request completes and its context is cancelled, the legacy write is cancelled mid-flight and the object exists only in unified storage. Mode 3's documented contract ('writing to LegacyStorage and Storage') is silently violated under load or client disconnects: legacy reads (dashboards, playlist legacy SQL paths) return stale/missing objects, and the divergence is invisible because the goroutine only logs.

[BUG] Update no longer wraps objInfo in updateWrapper before passing it to the legacy store, so the legacy Update receives the raw objInfo and computes/creates a possibly different object than the one unified storage wrote. Any Update where objInfo.UpdatedObject is not deterministic (e.g. reads current state, server-side defaults) writes divergent objects to legacy vs unified storage, breaking the dual-write consistency the mode exists to guarantee.

[BUG] Delete calls d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, ...) with the resource name where every other call site passes options.Kind, and Create/Update's storage-error paths call recordLegacyDuration(true, ..., startStorage) instead of recordStorageDuration. The dualwriter metrics this diff introduces emit mislabeled labels (error=true bucket, kind=object-name) for delete/create/update paths, corrupting every dashboard/alert built on these metrics and hiding real storage failures as 'legacy' failures.

[BUG] DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine records its duration with d.recordStorageDuration instead of d.recordLegacyDuration. Legacy DeleteCollection latency and failures are attributed to unified storage in the metrics, so an operator investigating slow/failed unified storage deletes sees phantom failures caused by legacy store outages.

[BUG] Delete's goroutine builds log via d.Log but passes ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) to the background write, while Delete also changed Delete semantics: legacy NotFound errors were previously tolerated (apierrors.IsNotFound check removed), so a legacy object deleted on one side now logs an error every time. The removed IsNotFound tolerance means every delete of an object that only ever existed in unified storage (created during mode 2/3 before migration) logs a spurious legacy delete error and is counted as a legacy failure in the new metrics.

[ADVISORY] The rewritten mode 3 tests only assert storage-path behavior and mock legacy success, with no test that the legacy goroutine write actually happens, fails, or is cancelled — the tests pass even if the legacy calls are deleted from the implementation. A future refactor that silently drops all legacy dual-writes (the core invariant of mode 3) passes CI; the async goroutines are completely untested, including their 10s timeout paths.

[ADVISORY] The new 'with dual write (etcd, mode 3)' integration test is added behind t.Skip, so it never runs in CI. The etcd mode 3 path — the production-relevant legacy backend — has zero executed coverage from this diff; regressions in mode 3 against etcd ship undetected to operators relying on etcd dual-write.

[ADVISORY] The refactor introduces per-method boilerplate (method string, log.WithValues, start timer, record call) duplicated across six methods with hand-maintained label combinations, which has already drifted (wrong record function in three places). The next mode or metric change must touch six near-identical blocks; the drift bugs already present in this diff demonstrate the maintenance hazard.

[BUG] Create's legacy write runs in a fire-and-forget goroutine whose context is derived from the request context, which is cancelled as soon as the request handler returns, so d.Legacy.Create executes with an already-cancelled context and fails with a context error every time. During mode-3 dual-write the legacy store never receives created objects; legacy and unified storage silently diverge with only a 10-second timeout error (not even logged) swallowed, so when operators later flip back or reconcile from legacy, data written during mode 3 is missing.

[BUG] Delete's success-path metrics call uses `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)`, passing the object name where every other call passes options.Kind, so the metric's kind label is the deleted object's name. Operators slicing dual-writer latency dashboards by kind get a garbage cardinality explosion (one label value per object name) and no per-kind storage-delete metrics; the same class of error appears in Update's failure path which calls recordLegacyDuration for a storage failure.

[BUG] Update's storage-failure path calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of recordStorageDuration, labeling failed unified-store update durations as legacy durations. Storage errors are recorded on the legacy metrics series, corrupting every latency/error-rate comparison the dual-write observability exists to provide, and no code in the diff or elsewhere consumes the mismatch to detect it.

[BUG] DeleteCollection's async legacy path calls `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)` for a Legacy.DeleteCollection call, recording legacy latencies on the storage series. Unified-store latency dashboards include legacy delete-collection timings, defeating the whole point of separate storage/legacy series; combined with the reversed mislabeling in Update this diff has no method where both series are correctly attributed for delete-collection/update.

[BUG] The goroutines share the caller's runtime.Object (Create) and rest.UpdatedObjectInfo/objInfo (Update) with the already-returned response object, so the legacy store mutates the same object the API response was serialized from while concurrent goroutines read it. Legacy storage implementations that stamp resourceVersion/UID/name on the passed object race with response serialization and with Update's objInfo being invoked a second time concurrently, producing torn reads or mutated response bodies; the previous synchronous design made this impossible.

[ADVISORY] Update no longer wraps objInfo in updateWrapper, so the legacy Update re-invokes objInfo.UpdatedObject against legacy's own old object instead of being forced to write the same object written to unified storage, and the two stores can legitimately compute and persist different contents. Any update whose function depends on the stored old state (defaulting, conflict resolution) writes different final objects to the two backends; migration completion checks comparing the two stores will report drift on every such update, and the old design's guarantee that legacy mirrored US is silently gone.

[ADVISORY] All legacy writes (Create, Delete, Update, DeleteCollection) are spawned as unbounded, unordered, best-effort goroutines with no retry, no queue, no dedup, and no error logging, so under load operations reach legacy out of order or not at all. An Update immediately followed by a Delete on the same object can be applied to legacy in reverse order, leaving a deleted object permanently present in legacy storage; a single dropped goroutine (process restart, 10s timeout) leaves an unrecoverable divergence with no reconciliation path, and burst traffic spawns one goroutine per write with no backpressure against the legacy backend.

[BUG] Create now performs the legacy-storage write in a fire-and-forget goroutine with a 10s timeout instead of the previous synchronous write, silently discarding legacy write failures and timed-out writes. When the legacy (SQL) store is slow or returns an error, the object exists only in unified storage; the dual-write contract that mode 3 keeps both stores consistent is broken with no error surfaced, and a legacy timeout silently abandons a write the caller believes was dual-written. No retry, no requeue, no metric on the dropped write beyond a latency label.

[BUG] Update no longer passes the updateWrapper carrying the object already computed for storage, so the async legacy Update re-evaluates objInfo against the legacy store's own current state instead of the same updated object. The old code guaranteed legacy received the exact object written to unified storage; now legacy Update derives its own object, so concurrent writes or legacy/store drift produce divergent objects between stores — the migration-intent invariant (legacy is a faithful copy until cutover) is silently removed with the wrapper.

[BUG] Delete drops the apierrors.IsNotFound tolerance for the legacy delete and makes it async, while previously a legacy NotFound was tolerated and any other legacy error was logged before returning the storage result. Objects created before mode 3 cutover (existing only in legacy) or already gone from legacy still delete fine from storage, but the async goroutine's error is dropped entirely — and more importantly the semantics changed from 'both stores deleted before return' to 'legacy deletion eventually attempted', so a caller completing Delete followed by a read from legacy during a rollback sees the object still present.

[BUG] DeleteCollection's async legacy path records its result via recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration, so legacy deletecollection latency and error rate are attributed to storage metrics. Operators watching the dual-writer dashboards see storage write failures that never happened and cannot see actual legacy deletecollection failures, defeating the observability this diff was meant to add.

[BUG] Update's storage-error path calls recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage), recording a storage failure as a legacy failure with storage's timestamp. Same metric-attribution corruption as above: update failures get counted against legacy, skewing the migration health signals used to decide whether mode 3 is safe to advance.

[ADVISORY] Delete builds a log with kind/name/method but then injects a different logger into the context (klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) without the WithValues), so all in-context log lines for delete lose name/kind/method correlation. On-call engineers debugging delete failures lose the object name from log lines; the per-call context that every other method in this file carefully attaches is silently discarded for delete only.

[ADVISORY] Create's error path returns created, err where created is the nil/failed result from Storage.Create, changing the previous contract which also returned the storage result but logged the legacy failure — the new code treats a storage failure as terminal while previously storage failure was also terminal, but now no legacy write is attempted at all on storage error. During a partial outage of unified storage, mode 3 previously still left a consistent-ish state via the legacy write not happening; the real consequence is weaker: the behavior change (no legacy fallback/attempt) is undocumented and no test covers the storage-failure-with-legacy path asserting legacy is not written, so a future edit re-adding a legacy write on storage error would pass CI silently.

[ADVISORY] Create dispatches the legacy-storage write to a fire-and-forget goroutine whose error is only logged, so legacy writes silently fail. During a mode-3 dual-write rollout, any legacy store failure (timeout after 10s, network error, etcd unavailable) leaves the two stores permanently divergent with no error surfaced to the caller and no retry; an operator later rolling back to mode 0/1 or reading via a legacy-only code path serves stale or deleted-then-resurrected objects to users, defeating the consistency the dual-write migration is meant to guarantee. Rebuttal gate: 'the legacy store is being retired anyway' — but the mode exists precisely because legacy readers are still live during migration, so silent divergence is a real failure mode, not a hypothetical.

[ADVISORY] Update passes the same objInfo (rest.UpdatedObjectInfo) concurrently to Storage.Update on the request goroutine and to Legacy.Update in the spawned goroutine after Storage.Update returns, so objInfo.UpdatedObject can be invoked concurrently/re-entrantly on shared state. If objInfo's underlying implementation holds mutable state (request-scoped caches, unguarded fields — the removed updateWrapper was exactly the guard this diff deleted), the background legacy update races and can compute a different object than the one written to unified storage, silently writing divergent data to legacy. Rebuttal gate: 'upstream objInfo is usually a pure closure' — plausible for the common path, but the wrapper that previously pinned the updated object was removed, and the API contract does not promise thread-safety of UpdatedObjectInfo; the deleted-guard deletion is observable in this diff.

[ADVISORY] Delete replaces the request context with klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) but without the per-request log values used in every other method, and Create's failure path labels storage durations as legacy durations. Delete's log line and metric lose the request-scoped correlation values that every other method in the file attaches, so security/audit investigation of a delete through mode 3 cannot correlate the log to the request; the Create/Update error paths emit metrics tagged as legacy failures when the failure was in unified storage, skewing the operational signal used to decide when it is safe to progress the migration. Rebuttal gate: 'metrics mislabeling is cosmetic' — it does not change runtime behavior, so advisory, but operators relying on these new metrics to gate mode progression get wrong data.

[BUG] TestMode3_Delete's happy-path case sets only a Storage mock expectation while DualWriterMode3.Delete fires a goroutine that calls d.Legacy.Delete, so the goroutine invokes an unmocked method on the shared testify mock and panics with "mock: I don't know what to return" from a non-test goroutine. Nondeterministic test process crash / data race depending on goroutine scheduling: the delete call in the goroutine hits legacyStoreMock's embedded *mock.Mock with no expectation, panicking asynchronously — the same holds for TestMode3_DeleteCollection, whose happy case also registers no legacy DeleteCollection expectation while the code dispatches one in a goroutine.

[BUG] The mode 3 tests never assert that the legacy write actually happened: no m.AssertExpectations(), no call-count check on LegacyStorage.Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection, and the happy-path assertions only check the object returned from Storage. Mode 3's defining behavior — dual-writing to legacy storage — is unverified. If the goroutine dispatch to d.Legacy.Create/Delete/Update is dropped or broken (e.g., the 10s-timeout context cancels before the call, or a future refactor removes the goroutine), every TestMode3_* test still passes green, so a silent loss of legacy replication ships. Checked: dualwriter_mode3_test.go is the only mode-3 spec in the diff; the original spy-based TestMode3 asserted lsSpy.Counts("LegacyStorage.Create") == 1 but the rewrite removed those assertions.

[BUG] TestMode3_Delete and TestMode3_Update never assert the returned async flag, and TestMode3_DeleteCollection never asserts the collection content returned matches the mock's exampleObj in a way distinguishable from the error case's early return path, while none of the tests exercise the goroutine timeout branch (10s context.WithTimeoutCause) or verify recordLegacyDuration/recordStorageDuration emitted correct metric labels (including the code's use of `name` instead of `options.Kind` in Delete's storage-duration call). The new metric-recording and timeout lifecycle paths added in this diff have zero triggering tests: a regression that mislabels duration metrics (Delete passes `name` where every other method passes `options.Kind`) or that leaks/cancels the legacy goroutine incorrectly is invisible to the suite. Checked: no other test file in the diff touches dualWriterMetrics or the legacy-timeout path.

[ADVISORY] The new "with dual write (file, mode 3)" and "with dual write (unified storage, mode 3)" integration subtests claim to cover dual-write but doPlaylistTests only reads through the API (which mode 3 serves from Storage), so nothing ever asserts the object also landed in legacy storage. Because mode 3 now writes legacy asynchronously in a fire-and-forget goroutine with a 10s timeout, these integration tests cannot and do not verify legacy replication: a regression that silently drops every legacy write in mode 3 (the goroutine never running, timeout firing, or the write erroring into the void) passes the full playlist integration suite. Checked playlist_test.go in the diff — the only dual-write-specific assertions anywhere are the mode-configuration plumbing in DualWriterDesiredModes.

[ADVISORY] The "with dual write (etcd, mode 3)" subtest is dead on arrival: it calls t.Skip("local etcd testing") as its first meaningful statement, so none of its mode-3 setup, DeleteCollection pre-clear, or doPlaylistTests body ever executes. Coverage reports and grep-based review show a mode-3 etcd dual-write test existing, but it executes zero assertions — false confidence for anyone relying on the suite covering mode 3 against etcd-backed legacy storage, the exact backend where the removed updateWrapper read-modify-write semantics and the new async legacy Update diverge most.

[BUG] The legacy Create is dispatched to a fire-and-forget goroutine whose context derives from the request context, so when the API handler returns the parent ctx is canceled and the legacy write fails or is abandoned mid-flight. Objects are committed to unified storage but never (or partially) written to legacy storage; a rollback/cutover back to legacy finds missing rows — silent data divergence during the migration window, with only a log line as evidence.

[BUG] The same async fire-and-forget pattern applies to Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection: the unified-store write succeeds and is returned to the client while the legacy-side delete/update runs in a detached goroutine that is never awaited, retried, or journaled. On process restart, goroutine panic, legacy timeout, or request-ctx cancellation, legacy storage keeps stale/undeleted rows, so any fallback to legacy (the entire point of dual-write) serves deleted or stale objects with no reconciliation path — data divergence that cannot be repaired from this code.

[BUG] Update passes the caller's original objInfo to the async legacy Update instead of the updateWrapper that syncs legacy to the unified-store result, dropping the divergence-guarding behavior the previous implementation had. Legacy Update re-evaluates objInfo against legacy's (possibly stale or divergent) old object, so legacy rows can be written with different contents than unified storage for the same update — the two stores silently diverge, and a later cutover back to legacy exposes stale data.

[BUG] Mode3 List now returns only Storage results, but no backfill/migration of pre-existing legacy rows into unified storage exists anywhere in this diff, so List/Get serve an incomplete dataset. Any resource already living only in legacy storage disappears from List (and Get after cutover) the moment Mode3 is enabled — pre-existing objects become invisible with no error, which is silent data loss from the user's perspective.

[BUG] On the Delete success path the code calls d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage), passing the object name where every other call passes the kind label. The delete duration metric gets cardinality-exploding per-object-name labels instead of kind, corrupting the migration observability dashboard and making the divergence between stores harder to detect.

[BUG] On the Update storage-error path the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) — recording a failed storage call as a legacy metric. Unified-store update failures are counted under the legacy metric, so the monitoring meant to catch dual-write divergence reports the wrong store failing.

[BUG] The DeleteCollection goroutine records its legacy-store call with d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...), so legacy delete-collection latency and errors are attributed to storage. Legacy DeleteCollection failures (which indicate divergent undeleted rows in legacy) are recorded as storage successes/failures, hiding the exact divergence signal this metric exists to surface.

[BUG] Create's legacy write is a fire-and-forget goroutine whose error is only recorded as a metric — no log, no retry, no surfaced failure. When d.Legacy.Create fails (or times out after 10s), the API returns success and the legacy store permanently diverges from unified storage with zero log line; operators discover it only via a metrics dashboard, and rollback to legacy storage serves stale/missing objects.

[BUG] Delete's legacy write is fire-and-forget with the error swallowed except for a metric counter. A legacy delete that fails or times out leaves the object present in legacy storage while the API reports the delete as successful; after downgrade or mode rollback the deleted object reappears, with no log or error to trace it.

[BUG] Update's legacy write is fire-and-forget with its error swallowed except for a metric. A failed legacy update leaves the old object version in legacy storage while the client sees the unified-store version; subsequent rollback reads stale data and no log exists to diagnose the divergence.

[BUG] DeleteCollection's legacy write is fire-and-forget with its error swallowed except for a metric. A failed or timed-out legacy DeleteCollection silently leaves a whole collection in legacy storage after the API reported successful deletion; divergence at collection scale with zero observability.

[BUG] The async legacy goroutines derive their context from the request-scoped ctx, which is cancelled as soon as the HTTP handler returns. Because the API responds immediately after the unified-store write and the goroutine runs after the handler completes, the apiserver cancels the request context before the legacy write finishes, so legacy writes routinely abort with context.Canceled — the dual write effectively never happens for slow legacy stores.

[BUG] Create's storage-failure path calls recordLegacyDuration instead of recordStorageDuration, attributing storage failures to the legacy metric. On a unified-store create failure, the legacy-failure metric is incremented, corrupting the operator-facing signal used to judge legacy health and migration readiness; the same wrong-recorder bug exists in Update's storage-error path (line ~138).

[BUG] DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine calls recordStorageDuration for a legacy operation, not recordLegacyDuration. Legacy delete-collection failures increment the storage metric, so dashboards show healthy legacy writes while they are actually failing (and vice versa).

[BUG] Delete records its metric with `name` in the kind label position (d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, ...)) instead of options.Kind. Every distinct object name becomes a distinct metric label value, exploding metric cardinality with per-object label sets and making the 'kind' label meaningless for the delete method; dashboards filtering by kind get per-name fragments.

[BUG] Update no longer uses updateWrapper, so the legacy write re-computes UpdatedObject from objInfo against legacy storage's own old state instead of persisting the object the unified store already accepted. If objInfo's transformation is not idempotent (e.g. timestamp regeneration, RV-derived defaults) or legacy's old object differs, legacy stores a different object version than unified storage — the exact skew updateWrapper existed to prevent — while both writes still 'succeed'.

Mode 3's documented contract ('writing to LegacyStorage and Storage') is silently violated under load or client disconnects: legacy reads (dashboards, playlist legacy SQL paths) return stale/missing objects, and the divergence is invisible because the goroutine only logs.

If the API request context is canceled/finished before the goroutine completes, the derived context is immediately canceled too, so `d.Legacy.Create(...)` may be aborted and never persist the object in legacy storage. The function also returns success based solely on `d.Storage.Create(...)` and does not surface legacy failure (only metrics), contradicting the mode comment "writing to LegacyStorage and Storage" and enabling silent divergence.

adjudication.rationale: In pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go, the previous Update implementation explicitly called objInfo.UpdatedObject(...) and used an updateWrapper to ensure the same computed object was used for subsequent writes (and then wrapped again to pass the actual object returned by unified storage to legacy). If objInfo is non-deterministic, legacy can compute a different object than what unified storage wrote, breaking dual-write consistency as the finding describes.

Because the API responds immediately after the unified-store write and the goroutine runs after the handler completes, the apiserver cancels the request context before the legacy write finishes, so legacy writes routinely abort with context.Canceled — the dual write effectively never happens for slow legacy stores.

adjudication.rationale: In Mode3 the legacy writes are now done asynchronously in goroutines (e.g., Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection) and each goroutine derives its context from the passed-in `ctx` via `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`. Because cancellation propagates from the parent context, if the caller cancels `ctx` after returning (common for request-scoped contexts), the legacy operation will be cancelled and can abort with `context.Canceled`, undermining the intended dual-write behavior for slower legacy stores.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Update no longer uses updateWrapper, so the legacy write re-computes UpdatedObject from objInfo against legacy storage's own old state instead of persisting the object the unified store already accepted. If objInfo's transformation is not idempotent (e.g. timestamp regeneration, RV-derived defaults) or legacy's old object differs, legacy stores a different object version than unified storage — the exact skew updateWrapper existed to prevent — while both writes still 'succeed'.

adjudication.rationale: In pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go, the Update implementation no longer computes the updated object once and wraps objInfo to reuse it for the legacy write. The previous code explicitly fetched old from Storage, computed `updated := objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, old)`, then used an `updateWrapper{updated: updated}` and, critically, passed a wrapper with `updated: obj` (the object returned/accepted by Storage.Update) into `d.Legacy.Update(...)`. The new code calls `d.Storage.Update(..., objInfo, ...)` and then asynchronously calls `d.Legacy.Update(..., objInfo, ...)` directly, meaning legacy will re-run objInfo’s transformation against legacy’s own prior state. If that transformation is non-idempotent or legacy state differs, unified and legacy can successfully persist divergent objects—exactly what updateWrapper prevented.
